power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 4 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: Kaplan-Meier curves comparing those who developed progressive CRS to those who did not show decreased survival in the progressive CRS group (p <0.001), Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>.
table.expanded: Kaplan-Meier curves comparing those who developed progressive CRS to those who did not show decreased survival in the progressive CRS group (p <0.001), Figure 2.

table.formatted: Those with progressive CRS who developed HF followed by ESKD and those with progressive CRS who developed ESKD followed by HF had decreased survival when compared to those without progressive CRS (p <0.0001), Figure <ref type="figure">3A</ref> and <ref type="figure">3B</ref>.
table.expanded: Those with progressive CRS who developed HF followed by ESKD and those with progressive CRS who developed ESKD followed by HF had decreased survival when compared to those without progressive CRS (p <0.0001), Figure 3A and 3B.

table.formatted: When the two subgroups were compared to each other there was no statistically significant difference seen in survival (p =0.25), Figure <ref type="figure">3C</ref>.
table.expanded: When the two subgroups were compared to each other there was no statistically significant difference seen in survival (p =0.25), Figure 3C.

table.formatted: Hazard ratios of progressive cardiorenal syndrome associated with traditional risk factors * Backward elimination method was used to select final model and only traditional risk factors that were significant (p<0.05) were retained.
table.expanded: Hazard ratios of progressive cardiorenal syndrome associated with traditional risk factors * Backward elimination method was used to select final model and only traditional risk factors that were significant (p<0.05) were retained.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.05", Text = "Hazard ratios of progressive cardiorenal syndrome associated with traditional risk factors * Backward elimination method was used to select final model and only traditional risk factors that were significant (p<0.05) were retained."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: When the two subgroups were compared to each other there was no statistically significant difference seen in survival (p =0.25), Figure <ref type="figure">3C</ref>.
table.expanded: When the two subgroups were compared to each other there was no statistically significant difference seen in survival (p =0.25), Figure 3C.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p =0.25", Sentence = "When the two subgroups were compared to each other there was no statistically significant difference seen in survival (p =0.25), Figure 3C."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
